title: South Korea's robot agency and LG plan pilot safety certification for humanoids
excerpt: South Korea's state robot agency will pilot safety certification with LG's humanoid robots and build tests for stability, AI reliability and cybersecurity.

sources.title: Seoul Economic Daily: Korea Robot Agency, LG Electronics team up on humanoid robot safety (16 November 2026)
JKN: LG Electronics and Korea Institute for Robot Industry Advancement sign agreement to pursue domestic safety pilot certification for humanoids (16 November 2026)
Humanoids Daily: LG signs with Korea's robot certification agency to safety-test its humanoids (16 November 2026)
Etnews: Daegu humanoid robot safety certification centre project on track (5 August 2026, Korean)

body_html:
South Korea's state robot agency and LG Electronics have agreed to work together on how humanoid robots are tested for safety before they are sold. The agreement was signed on 13 November 2026 at LG's offices in Seoul and announced on 16 November 2026.

The agency is the Korea Institute for Robot Industry Advancement (KIRIA), a government body that runs South Korea's robot certification programmes. Humanoid robots are machines built roughly in the shape of a person, usually with arms and often with legs, and designed to work in spaces made for people, such as homes and factories.

What the agreement covers

According to reports of the announcement, the two sides agreed to three things:

  • A pilot safety certification. LG will put its humanoid robots, including the CLOiD robot it is developing, through a domestic pilot of safety certification.
  • Help building the test system. LG's product quality standards and experience will feed into the evaluation system for a humanoid safety certification centre that KIRIA is setting up.
  • Standards work. Both will contribute to national and international standards for humanoid robots.

The reports say the aim is to check risks and quality early in development, "rather than merely verifying safety after a product is completed". Areas to be evaluated include safety and ease of use when people and robots work together, as well as how the robots move and how their AI behaves. KIRIA's president, Cho Young-hoon, was quoted as saying that trust in safety and quality matters more than anything else.

The certification centre behind it

The centre is being built at South Korea's National Robot Test Field in Daegu, in the south-east of the country, after Daegu won a national competition run by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. Korean technology news site Etnews reported a budget of 18.65 billion won (roughly 13 million US dollars) from 2026 to 2030, mostly from national and city funds. The centre is planned to test three things: dynamic stability (whether a robot stays upright and controlled while moving), AI reliability and cybersecurity. Testing, field trials and certification are meant to happen in one place.

The centre is also meant to help Korean makers prepare for European rules, in particular the EU AI Act and the EU Cyber Resilience Act, which sets security requirements for connected products.

What is still unknown

The reports do not say which tests LG's robots will face, which existing standards (for example ISO robot safety standards) the pilot will use, when the pilot will finish, or whether other humanoid makers will take part. South Korea has no formal safety certification scheme for humanoids yet; a pilot is a step towards one, not a finished scheme. We could not open LG's own press release, so this story relies on Korean news reports of it.

Why it matters for staying in charge

A humanoid that walks has a particular safety problem: it cannot always just cut its power and freeze, because it may fall. Testing how a robot stops, keeps its balance and behaves near people is central to Directive 1, always stoppable, and Directive 3, physical safety. Including cybersecurity in the tests reflects Directive 6, secure and supported: a hacked robot is one nobody is in charge of.

Putting a product through outside testing early, before it reaches homes, also supports Directive 9, accountable: someone has checked the claims and someone answers for the result. Agreements like this one are part of how standards for a new kind of machine get written, and they work best when the tests and results are published so that buyers can see what was checked.

When humanoid robots go on sale, buyers can ask any maker the questions on our questions to ask page, such as how the robot is stopped, what happens when it loses power, and who tested it.
